title: Review: The periodic table
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.1.2-c20, 4.1.2-c16, 4.1.2-c05, 4.1.2-c14. Clues: 4.1.2-c20 written for the game from the bank's definition; 4.1.2-c16 written for the game from the bank's definition; 4.1.2-c05 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.1.2-c14 first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.1.2-q02, 4.1.2-q09, 4.1.2-q30, 4.1.2-q05, 4.1.2-q07, 4.1.2-q10, 4.1.2-q04, 4.1.2-q06, 4.1.2-q14, 4.1.2-q03, 4.1.2-q08, 4.1.2-q11. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Diatomic molecule
items.clue: Two atoms joined together, such as Cl2 or Br2.

items.label: Alkali metals
items.clue: The elements of Group 1, each with one outer electron.

items.label: Outer electrons
items.clue: The electrons in the highest occupied shell of an atom.

items.label: Stable electron arrangement
items.clue: An outer shell holding eight electrons, or two in the case of helium, so the atom has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.

questions.stem: Why is the table of the elements described as periodic?

options.text: Because the table is revised at regular periods as new elements appear
Because elements with similar properties recur at regular intervals
Because every row repeats the properties of the row above it
Because each element repeats the electron count before it

questions.explanation: The specification says the table is called periodic because similar properties occur at regular intervals along it.

questions.stem: Knowledge of isotopes helped chemists understand the periodic table. What exactly did it explain?

options.text: Why atomic weights could be measured far more precisely
Why two atoms of one element hold different protons
Why an order based on atomic weights is not always correct
Why Mendeleev's swapped pairs were mistakes after all

questions.explanation: Isotope mixtures mean atomic weight does not always rise with proton number, which explains the pairs Mendeleev had to swap.

questions.stem: An atom of element Q has 19 protons. What does an atom of Q do when it reacts?

options.text: Loses one electron to form a 1+ ion
Loses its outer electron, giving a 1- ion
Gains seven electrons to form a 7- ion
Loses four electrons to make a 4+ ion

questions.explanation: 19 protons means 19 electrons, arranged 2,8,8,1. The single outer electron is lost, so Q is a metal forming a 1+ ion.

questions.stem: Rubidium lies below potassium in Group 1. From its position, what can be predicted about its reaction with water?

options.text: It reacts less vigorously than potassium, being a heavier metal
It reacts more vigorously than potassium, giving off hydrogen gas
It reacts to give rubidium oxide along with hydrogen gas
It reacts much like strontium, its neighbour in that period

questions.explanation: Reactivity increases down Group 1, so rubidium reacts more vigorously than potassium and gives rubidium hydroxide and hydrogen.

questions.stem: What problem arose in the early periodic tables when the strict order of atomic weights was followed?

options.text: Faulty weight values scattered elements far from their true partners
The atomic weights themselves had all been measured wrongly
Permanent gaps appeared that no element could ever fill
Some elements were placed in groups they did not belong in

questions.explanation: The specification states that early tables were incomplete and that strict weight order put some elements in inappropriate groups.

questions.stem: Sodium reacts to form Na+ ions and sulfur does not form positive ions. What does this tell you about them?

options.text: Sodium is a non-metal and sulfur is a metal
Sodium must be a non-metal, because it forms a positive ion
Both are non-metals, since neither formed a negative ion
Sodium is a metal and sulfur is a non-metal element

questions.explanation: Elements that react to form positive ions are metals; elements that do not form positive ions are non-metals.

questions.stem: An atom of element X has the electronic structure 2,8,7. Where in the periodic table is X found?

options.text: Group 3 and Period 7, reading its three occupied shells
Group 17 and Period 3, counting all the electrons
Group 3 and Period 3, since the shell count gives both
Group 7 and Period 3, from seven outer electrons

questions.explanation: Seven electrons in the outer shell places X in Group 7, and three occupied shells places it in Period 3.

questions.stem: Before protons, neutrons and electrons were discovered, how did scientists attempt to classify the elements?

options.text: By arranging them in order of the atomic number
By arranging them in order of their outer electron counts
By arranging them in order of their atomic weights
By arranging them in order of their neutron count

questions.explanation: The specification states that before those particles were known, scientists classified elements by ordering them by atomic weight.

questions.stem: Why does magnesium react to form Mg2+ ions while chlorine reacts to form Cl- ions?

options.text: Magnesium loses its two outer electrons; chlorine gains one
Magnesium gains six electrons and chlorine loses seven
Magnesium has more protons than chlorine has in total
Magnesium has outer electrons it readily gives away

questions.explanation: Reactions follow the arrangement of electrons: an atom with few outer electrons loses them, one with a nearly full shell gains.

questions.stem: Chlorine and bromine are both in Group 7 and react in similar ways. What do atoms of these two elements share?

options.text: The same total number of electrons in the whole atom
The same number of occupied shells in the atom
The same number of outer electrons in an atom
The same number of neutrons in the nucleus

questions.explanation: Elements in one group have the same number of outer electrons, and that is what gives them similar chemical properties.

questions.stem: Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table. Why did he do this?

options.text: He expected undiscovered elements to fill them
He believed that no element could ever exist there
He thought those places in nature were forever empty
He was unsure of several measured atomic weights

questions.explanation: Mendeleev overcame some of the problems by leaving gaps for elements he thought had not yet been discovered.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes where metals and non-metals sit in the periodic table?

options.text: Most elements are metals, on the left and lower down
Most elements are metals, on the right near the top
Most elements are non-metals, on the left and lower down
Most elements are non-metals, over on the right

questions.explanation: The majority of elements are metals, found to the left and towards the bottom, with non-metals towards the right and top.
